profiles.meeting_scenario: A mid-project planning meeting at a game studio building a third-person stealth game, where the team wants to adopt an Agile Behaviour Design-style workflow for enemy NPCs in the next milestone. The immediate context is planning a two-week implementation slice for a new 'courtyard guard' behavior set so designers can iterate on interactions without waiting on engine changes. The agenda is to agree on what the first vertical slice includes, how the behavior authoring pipeline will be set up, who owns each part of the work, and what must be ready by the milestone review. The expected outcome is a shared plan covering the initial behavior tree scaffolding, the designer-facing behavior stubs, the integration path into the existing AI stack, and a delivery timeline for something both consider a usable first pass.

members.name: Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: NPC architecture, behavior trees, Unreal AI integration, build and debug tooling
members.background: Lena has spent six years shipping action and stealth titles and recently inherited the studio's AI framework after a partial engine upgrade. She is comfortable building extensible systems and wants to reduce ad hoc requests from design by introducing cleaner interfaces.
members.private_state: She wants to protect engineering time by defining a minimal, stable integration path that designers can use without repeatedly changing core code. She is also worried about performance regressions in the existing perception stack and wants the milestone to be judged on technical readiness rather than content completeness.
hidden_assumptions: A 'first pass' for the guard behavior means the full runtime path exists end-to-end in-engine, even if many actions are placeholder implementations.
When people say designers can 'work independently,' they mean designers can author and reorder behavior nodes inside a constrained schema that engineering exposes first.
The 'courtyard guard' slice naturally includes the production perception and alert-state pipeline because otherwise the behavior cannot be meaningfully validated.
If a behavior is 'playable' for milestone review, it should survive a normal game build, navmesh, save/load, and basic profiling without engineer supervision.

members.name: Marcus Feld
members.expertise: Encounter design, systemic NPC behaviors, scripting workflows, cross-discipline prototyping
members.background: Marcus came from a studio with heavy designer-owned scripting and has been advocating for a more Agile Behaviour Design-like process so encounter designers can sketch interactions earlier. He often works backward from player-facing moments and is used to proving concepts with mocked reactions before systems are fully connected.
members.private_state: He wants a planning outcome that gives design room to experiment with guard reactions and patrol interruptions quickly, without being blocked on engineering details. He is concerned that if the milestone is framed too technically, design will lose another sprint waiting for robust infrastructure before testing any interesting interactions.
hidden_assumptions: A 'first pass' means designers can stage believable interaction beats in the editor, even if some transitions are faked or manually triggered for now.
When people say designers can 'work independently,' they mean design should be able to define new guard sequences and test them without filing engineering tickets for every missing action.
The 'courtyard guard' slice mainly covers the authored interaction loop in the courtyard encounter, not every production system the same NPC will eventually depend on elsewhere.
If something is 'playable' for milestone review, it only needs to communicate the intended player experience in a controlled demo map.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to deliver a 'first pass' of the courtyard guard behavior by the milestone review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an end-to-end integrated implementation in the main AI framework, with placeholder leaf actions allowed but real sensing, state transitions, and game-loop execution wired up.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a designer-iterable prototype of the guard's patrol, inspect, and investigate beats that can be demoed convincingly, even if some transitions are editor-driven or temporarily mocked.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In game development, 'first pass' is a routine phrase that often intentionally tolerates incompleteness, so both hear healthy flexibility rather than a need to define exactly what kind of incompleteness is allowed.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss building the 'courtyard guard' slice for this sprint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this slice includes all reusable runtime dependencies the guard needs in shipping contexts, especially perception hookup, alert escalation, animation event calls, and save-safe state handling.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this slice is bounded to the courtyard encounter itself, so locally scripted triggers, simplified alert flow, and map-specific setups are acceptable as long as the encounter can be iterated on.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about the same named NPC and map area, so the label feels concrete enough; neither realizes the other is using a different boundary for what work naturally 'belongs' to that slice.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the guard behavior should be 'playable' by Thursday's internal milestone check.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'playable' means the behavior runs in the shared branch inside the standard gameplay test map under normal QA conditions, without manual setup beyond documented console flags.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'playable' means the encounter team can walk reviewers through the intended sequence in the courtyard demo level, even if some setup steps or hidden triggers are needed behind the scenes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use 'playable' as a common milestone adjective, and in creative teams it often bundles many informal expectations; because both are cooperative, each assumes the other's threshold is close enough.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Lena will expose the needed 'stubs' so Marcus can start authoring behaviors independently.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes 'stubs' are engineer-created leaf-task interfaces and blackboard keys generated in C++ and registered in the behavior editor before designers touch them.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'stubs' include lightweight designer-side placeholder actions and conditions that he can create directly in the scripting layer, with engineering filling in runtime details later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'stub' implies temporary scaffolding to both sides, and because Agile Behaviour Design explicitly emphasizes decoupling design from implementation, each thinks their own workflow interpretation is the obvious one.

turns.inner_thought: I need to frame this so we stop treating the milestone like a content sketch and actually land the runtime path. A first pass of the courtyard guard behavior has to mean it's really in the game loop, using the proper AI framework, even if some leaf tasks are placeholders. If we don't include the real dependencies now, we'll just pay for it twice when design starts asking why the prototype falls apart outside the demo.
turns.utterance: Okay, for this sprint I'd like us to line up a first pass of the courtyard guard for the next milestone and do it in a way that doesn't box us in later. If we set the shape of it now, we should be able to expand without redoing the whole thing.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as 'courtyard guard' stays focused on the encounter and not on every system dependency in the AI stack. What I need out of this is room for design to try patrol breaks, inspect beats, and distraction reactions quickly. If we can work independently once the scaffolding exists, we can stop waiting on engineering every time we want to test a new guard sequence.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that works for me. The big thing from design's side is that the courtyard guard slice lets us start iterating independently on patrol, inspect, and distraction reactions in that encounter. If we can get to that, we'll learn a lot faster.

turns.inner_thought: I should lock down ownership now. 'Stubs' means I expose the leaf-task interfaces, blackboard contract, and the editor-visible nodes from engineering first, so design isn't inventing temporary logic that later has to be unwound. Stable skeleton first, then Marcus can reorder and tune within that lane.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. What I'd like to do, then, is expose the needed stubs early so you can author against a stable behavior skeleton while I wire the runtime path underneath it. That way you're not waiting on the full implementation before you can start shaping things.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. If Lena gets the stubs in, I can start filling them right away with placeholder actions and rough conditions in the designer layer, just enough to sketch the flow. A first pass doesn't need every transition to be fully connected yet; it needs to let us test whether the guard beats feel right.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that's ideal. Once those stubs are there, I can start filling them in right away with placeholder pieces and get the interaction flow on its feet. That should get us to a first pass pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: I need to put a marker down on scope without turning this into an argument. For the courtyard guard slice to be worth anything, it has to include perception hookup, alert escalation, and animation event hooks in the real stack. Otherwise we'll have a pretty-looking tree that tells us nothing about performance or whether the state machine survives actual gameplay conditions.
turns.utterance: One thing I do want folded into the courtyard guard slice from the start is the perception side, the alert escalation, and the animation event hooks. I don't want us proving out the behavior in a vacuum and then discovering the core loop changes once it's plugged in.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as it doesn't turn into a blocker. For the first pass, if the courtyard loop is playable, I'm happy to use local triggers and a simplified setup to get the beats in front of people. We can clean up the plumbing later once we've validated the player-facing sequence actually works.
turns.utterance: Totally fair. From my side, as long as the courtyard loop is playable, I'm okay with us using whatever gets the first pass moving and then cleaning up as we go. The main thing is getting the sequence into a form we can react to.

turns.inner_thought: I should anchor the milestone in something testable. 'Playable' by Thursday needs to mean it's on the shared branch, running in the normal path, and solid enough that QA can smoke-test it without me standing over their shoulder. Otherwise review day turns into a hand-held demo and nobody notices the actual integration gaps.
turns.utterance: Alright, then let's use Thursday as the checkpoint. By the internal milestone check, the guard behavior should be playable so QA can smoke-test it in the shared branch before we walk into review.

turns.inner_thought: Thursday is good. I can absolutely have a playable courtyard demo sequence by then, with the investigation beats and a recover-to-patrol loop in place, even if some of the setup is still controlled. That gives review something concrete to respond to without design losing another sprint to infrastructure.
turns.utterance: Thursday works. I'll make sure we have a playable courtyard sequence for review by then, including the investigation beats and the recover-to-patrol loop, so people can see the behavior arc end to end.

turns.inner_thought: Let's make ownership explicit. I'll handle the tree skeleton, blackboard keys, and engine-side stubs in C++ and get them registered properly. Marcus can focus on ordering nodes and encounter logic within that contract. If we separate it cleanly, engineering time stays protected and design gets a stable lane to work in.
turns.utterance: For ownership, I'll take the behavior tree skeleton, the blackboard contract, and the stubs on my side. Once that's in, can you own the node ordering and the encounter logic against that setup?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that's the plan I wanted: design starts independent authoring as soon as the stubs land, and we use the courtyard review on Thursday to show the first pass in motion. As long as I can keep extending the guard sequence without new tickets every few hours, this is a workable Agile Behavior Design step.
turns.utterance: Yep, that's a good split. As soon as the stubs land, design will start authoring independently, and we'll aim to have the first pass ready for the courtyard review on Thursday.
